verified.name: Cajueiro de Pirangi (The Cashew of Pirangi)

location.address: Pirangi do Norte beach, Parnamirim, Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil, 12 km south of Natal

verified.access: Paid entry, R$10 (electronic payment only), open daily 8:00-17:30 (10:00-17:30 on Jan 1 and Dec 25, closed on election days). Walkways and a viewing tower let visitors see the whole crown.
verified.transport: 12 km south of Natal via Via Costeira then RN-063 (Rota do Sol); no rail, drive or taxi/bus, roughly 20-25 minutes from central Natal
verified.verify_notes: Single specimen, not a grove: a genetic anomaly makes its branches grow laterally and re-root on touching the ground, so one tree has spread to cover 7,300-9,000 sq m (sources vary; pt.wikipedia says ~8,500 sqm, a 2025 news report says 'about 9,000 sqm, the size of a football pitch'), described as the equivalent of 70 ordinary cashew trees with a c.500m perimeter. Planted in 1888 by fisherman Luis Inacio de Oliveira, who according to local tradition died at 93 beneath its branches (repeated across sources, treat as folklore-adjacent but the planting date itself is the commonly cited figure). Entered Guinness World Records in 1994 as the world's largest cashew tree; a competing tree in Piaui state (Cajueiro da Praia) claims a larger area (~8,800 sqm) in a 2016 state tourism study but was never Guinness-measured, so Pirangi keeps the record. As of 2025 the tree's spreading branches are pressing into the adjacent Rota do Sol highway, a live maintenance concern, and ticketing/hours were updated Nov 2025, both of which confirm it is an actively managed, currently standing attraction. No trunk girth applies in any normal sense since the whole point of the tree is its lateral spread rather than a single trunk; do not force a girth figure onto it. By far the strongest candidate of this batch: Guinness-recognised, 6-language Wikipedia coverage, ~2845 reads/month, an unambiguous single collectible destination with its own gate and ticket booth. Clears the single-tree-destination test easily.
verified.destination_test: PASS: a Guinness World Record holder ('world's largest cashew tree'), ticketed, signposted, actively visited attraction with its own entrance and viewing tower. People plan trips from Natal specifically to see it.

verified.name: O Patriarca (Patriarca da Floresta)

location.address: Pe de Gigante section, Parque Estadual Vassununga, Santa Rita do Passa Quatro, Sao Paulo state, Brazil
location.neighbourhood: Pe de Gigante, Vassununga State Park

verified.access: Free entry, but advance online registration through the park's own form is mandatory. Open daily 8:00-16:00. Pets not allowed; terrain is not accessible for mobility-limited visitors. Reachable via marked trails, sometimes with environmental monitor guides.
verified.transport: In Santa Rita do Passa Quatro, Sao Paulo state, about 244 km from the city of Sao Paulo; reached by car via SP-348 (Rodovia dos Bandeirantes) then SP-050. No public transport to the park gate identified.
verified.verify_notes: Widely reported as the oldest tree in Brazil (multiple outlets use exactly that framing). Species Cariniana legalis, a jequitiba-rosa, in the Pe de Gigante cerrado section (900 ha) of Vassununga State Park. Height reported inconsistently: English Wikipedia's derived source gives 40m, one Portuguese source gives 42m, another 49m; pick 40-42m as the likely honest range for the writer and flag the outlier. Circumference reported as 11.5m in one source and 12.3m in another (both convert to a diameter of 3.6-4m, roughly 13 people needed to link arms around it); recorded girth_cm as 1150 (11.5m) as the more conservative, English-Wikipedia-sourced figure, note the 1230cm alternative for the writer. AGE IS THE BIGGEST DISAGREEMENT IN THIS BATCH: English Wikipedia's own article notes the 600-year figure comes from comparing it to a NEIGHBOURING tree that was carbon-14 dated (a bridge claim risk: that comparison is not a direct dating of the Patriarca itself), while the municipality claims 1,000 years and other outlets repeat a carbon-14 claim of 'over 3,000 years' directly. Do not silently pick one; the story should say the tree is uncounted-centuries old and known locally as Brazil's oldest, without committing to a single number. Location precision only approximate: coordinate comes from the Commons/Wikidata lead only, not confirmed against a park trail map or geotagged photo, and the Pe de Gigante section is large; a future pass should pin it against the park's own trail map. Access requires pre-booking, which is honestly stated rather than a blocker under hard rule 10's three tests (no permission from a private party needed, just a state park's own booking system, comparable to a museum timed ticket).
verified.destination_test: PASS, with a caveat: consistently reported in Brazilian press as the country's oldest tree, a genuine draw ('veja a arvore mais antiga do pais'). Weaker demand signal than Pirangi (2 language Wikipedias, ~97 reads/month) but the fame is real and specific to this one named tree, not a park population.

verified.name: Baikushev's Pine (Baikushevata Mura)

location.address: Pirin National Park, near Banderitsa hut, about 12-15 km from Bansko, Blagoevgrad Province, Bulgaria

verified.access: Free, inside Pirin National Park, no permit needed for this well-established site. Reachable by car (parking area about 400m past Banderitsa hut), on foot (about 3.5 hours / 12.6 km from Bansko for the full hike), by bicycle, or by bus running to Banderitsa hut. A fenced viewing area and wooden stairs are built around the tree.
verified.transport: About 12-15 km from Bansko; roughly 30 minutes by car via Pirin Street to Banderitsa hut, or about 3.5 hours on foot from Bansko town
verified.verify_notes: Named after forest ranger Kostadin Baikushev who identified it. Considered one of the oldest trees in Europe; sources repeat 'contemporary with Khan Asparukh', founder of the First Bulgarian Empire (c. 681 AD), which is where the ~1,300-year figure likely traces to, though no source found states the dating METHOD (ring count vs estimate); treat the age as a repeated, widely-cited figure rather than a freshly derived one, per the vague-source rule. Height 24m, diameter 2.22m, circumference 7.8m (recorded as girth_cm 780). Strong Wikipedia coverage (10 languages, ~1318 reads/month), the clear strongest Bulgarian candidate. No dated recent news found confirming continued life, but the tree is an established, maintained tourist site with built infrastructure (fence, stairs, parking, bus stop), which is itself a strong continued-standing signal; no death/storm reports found in searching.
verified.destination_test: PASS: one of the most famous named trees in Bulgaria, a specific hiking/driving destination within Pirin National Park with its own signage, parking and viewing platform, and the strongest Bulgarian demand signal by far (10 language Wikipedias).
